# Chapter 8 — Governance Is Not a Point in Time

*The Drift Detection Requirement.*

## The Temporal Nature of Governance State

A foundational distinction runs through every chapter of this document, but it has not yet been stated explicitly: governance is not a configuration event. It is a continuous condition. An organization that correctly configures its policy assignments on a given day, correctly populates every identity's position attribute, correctly maintains every dynamic group, and correctly documents every infrastructure dependency, and then makes no further governance investments in the weeks and months that follow, will find that the real-world state of its environment has diverged from its intended governance state. Not because anyone made errors. Not because any tools failed. But because the environment is not static, and a governance model that is not continuously maintained cannot remain accurate against a continuously changing reality.

Users move between organizational units when they change roles. New users are onboarded, and the onboarding process does not always follow the governed enrollment workflow that populates the position attribute correctly. Devices are provisioned — sometimes through approved Autopilot workflows, sometimes through manual enrollment by local administrators who do not know about the position attribute requirement. Servers are added to resource groups without the correct organizational position tags, because the engineer who provisioned them was focused on the workload, not on the governance tagging convention. Dynamic group membership rules are modified by administrators who need to solve an immediate policy targeting problem without understanding that the rule is part of a governed hierarchy representation. Service accounts accumulate permissions through ad-hoc privileged access requests that are approved individually but never reviewed collectively. The environment drifts, continuously and in many dimensions simultaneously.

## Why Cloud-Native Drift Is Qualitatively Different

Drift is not a new problem. Active Directory environments drifted too — computer objects in wrong OUs, users in incorrect security groups, GPOs linked to OUs they should not have been linked to. The significant difference is that in an Active Directory environment, structural drift was visible. The OU tree was the record of intended structure. An administrator who wanted to know whether a computer object was in the wrong OU could compare the object's current OU path against the OU path that the governance model specified for objects of its type. The tree was both the governance model and the data — and because they were the same artifact, comparing current state against intended state was a tractable operation, requiring directory inspection rather than cross-reference against a separate authority document.

In the cloud-native model, the intended state exists only as an intention — unless it has been explicitly encoded in a governed, machine-readable artifact. If the organizational hierarchy registry described in Chapter 3 does not exist, there is nothing to compare the current state of identity attributes against. If an identity's position attribute carries a value that was valid twelve months ago but references an organizational node that was renamed or restructured since then, there is no mechanism to detect that the value is now stale. The attribute still contains a string. The string is no longer consistent with the current hierarchy. But because there is no authoritative registry of valid paths to compare against, the staleness is invisible — not because nothing has changed, but because there is no reference against which to measure the change.

This invisibility is the qualitative difference between drift in an Active Directory environment and drift in a cloud-native governance model built on the architecture described in this document. In the Active Directory environment, structural drift was visible in the tree. In the cloud-native model, structural drift is invisible unless a drift detection capability is built that continuously compares live state against the authoritative registry. Without that capability, the governance model degrades silently over time, and the degradation is not recoverable without a full audit — which is expensive, disruptive, and typically performed only after the degradation has already caused a governance failure.

## Drift Detection as a Continuous Governance Operation

The drift detection capability that the governance substrate must include is not a manual periodic audit. It is an automated, scheduled process that runs continuously against the live directory state, comparing every identity's organizational position attribute against the current state of the hierarchy registry, and producing a classified inventory of detected deviations. The classification must distinguish between different categories of drift: attributes that contain values not present in the current registry — which may indicate a stale value from a hierarchy restructuring; identities that have no organizational position attribute populated at all — which indicates an enrollment governance failure; position attributes whose path structure is syntactically invalid — which indicates a data quality problem in the attribute derivation process; and group memberships that do not match the group memberships that should be derived from the current position attribute values — which indicates that the dynamic group library has not been kept current with the registry.

Each category of drift has a different remediation profile. Stale path values require attribute updates that propagate registry changes to the affected identity objects. Missing attributes require enforcement of enrollment governance. Syntactically invalid attributes require investigation of the provisioning workflow that generated them. Group membership inconsistencies require investigation of the dynamic group rules and their alignment with the registry. The drift detection report must surface these distinctions, and it must do so in machine-readable form that can be committed to the version-controlled governance record, so that the history of drift events — when deviations arose, what their nature was, when they were remediated — is preserved as part of the organization's governance audit trail.

::: {.callout-note title="Architectural Requirement — Chapter 8"}
The governance substrate must include a continuous drift detection capability. The authoritative hierarchy registry must serve as the baseline against which the current state of every identity's organizational position attribute is compared on a scheduled basis. Deviations must be detected, classified by type and severity, and surfaced for remediation. Drift detection must be automated, not manual. Its outputs must be machine-readable and committed to a version-controlled governance record, so that the history of drift events is auditable independently of the live directory state at any given moment.
:::
